headline_findings: This comparison is based on exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, so it describes what these two specific papers show, not Lyme disease or Long COVID in general.

Both papers independently find that official counting systems substantially undercount the true number of people affected, though they measure this undercount in very different ways and neither paper reports any cost, income-loss, or caregiving burden data.

The Long COVID paper uniquely documents who gets left out of diagnosis codes (by sex, race, and neighborhood poverty) and how long it took for a diagnosis code to even exist, while the Lyme disease paper uniquely quantifies a large numeric gap between claims-based diagnosis estimates and surveillance case counts.

comparison_rows.dimension: Scale of the gap between official case counts and the real number of people diagnosed/coded

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper estimates about 476,744.19 diagnosed-and-treated patients/year from insurance claims, compared with roughly 35,000 surveillance-reported cases/year, a 13.62 claims-to-surveillance ratio; the authors say this gap reflects a mix of underreporting and overdiagnosis they cannot separate.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not produce a comparable national diagnosed-vs-surveillance ratio; instead it shows that 37.2% of the coded cohort had no recorded acute-infection date and that the diagnosis code itself took about 2 years to become available, both pointing to undercounting through a different mechanism.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Readers should not treat the two conditions as undercounted in the same way or by the same magnitude -the Lyme figure is a national scale comparison, the Long COVID figure is about data completeness within a coded cohort.

comparison_rows.dimension: Reliance on insurance claims/diagnosis codes as the data source

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper's entire estimate comes from commercial insurance claims identified by ICD codes, with a correction factor because many medical records meeting clinical criteria lacked the Lyme-specific code (only 43.0% of 672 reviewed records had it).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper's entire cohort comes from presence of the U09.9 diagnosis code in electronic health record data, and the paper states usage mixes billing and clinical contexts that cannot be distinguished, with eligible patients likely missing the code entirely.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers' core numbers depend on imperfect diagnosis coding, so both are vulnerable to the same kind of undercounting from coding gaps rather than true absence of disease.

comparison_rows.dimension: Delay before a usable diagnosis code or case definition existed

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper does not report any figure for how long a diagnosis code or case definition took to become available.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports roughly 2 years between patients first describing symptoms (Spring 2020) and the dedicated U09.9 code becoming available (October 2021), during which ad hoc placeholder coding was used.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Long COVID paper gives direct evidence that a coding/classification delay itself created an early period of invisibility in the data.

comparison_rows.dimension: Demographic representation gaps in who gets diagnosed or coded

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports no sex, race, ethnicity, or income breakdown of its 476,744.19/year estimate; this is explicitly flagged as not reported.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper finds the coded cohort was 11.3 percentage points more female and 10.7 percentage points more White than the broader SARS-CoV-2-positive population at the same sites, indicating under-representation of men and non-White patients among those captured.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Long COVID paper shows which groups are likely missing from the counted population, which matters for knowing who official data underserves.

comparison_rows.dimension: Socioeconomic or geographic access barriers to being diagnosed/counted

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports a 14-percentage-point difference in low-incidence-state diagnosis share versus typical surveillance share, but frames this as possible overdiagnosis rather than an access barrier, and reports no income or area-poverty data.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports that the coded cohort had a modestly higher share from low-poverty-rate neighborhoods (29.6% vs 26.3% among all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients), suggesting patients in more deprived areas were less likely to receive the code despite the paper noting higher underlying COVID-19 rates there.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Long COVID paper directly links neighborhood-level economic disadvantage to being left out of the diagnosed/counted population.

comparison_rows.dimension: Out-of-pocket or direct medical cost evidence

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports no dollar cost figures of any kind -no cost per diagnosis, treatment cost, or out-of-pocket spending.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper likewise reports no direct medical cost, non-medical cost, or out-of-pocket spending figures anywhere.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Neither paper can answer 'how much does this cost patients,' so any cost-of-illness claim about either condition would need an external, clearly labeled cost source not present in either paper.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper contains no data on missed work, income loss, or productivity impact.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper contains no individual-level employment or income-loss data, only an ecological area-level unemployment-rate proxy mentioned as a factor still needing study.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both conditions' work/income burden remains entirely unmeasured by these two papers, which matters for anyone trying to size the economic impact on patients.

comparison_rows.dimension: What the evidence leaves unmeasured overall

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper explicitly states it does not address delayed diagnosis, repeated care-seeking, persistent-symptom (post-treatment) burden, caregiving time, or any subgroup breakdown of its national estimate.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper explicitly states it does not address caregiver strain, insurance-denial experiences, individual-level financial consequences, or a national prevalence estimate.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers leave the lived financial and caregiving burden of these conditions completely undescribed, so neither can be used on its own to estimate total economic burden.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers find that the official, publicly reported counting system substantially undercounts the people actually affected, though by different mechanisms and without a precise, agreed-upon 'true' number.

evidence.note: Finds roughly 13.62 times more claims-based diagnosed-and-treated patients (about 476,744.19/year) than the approximately 35,000 cases/year reported through passive surveillance, while stating it cannot separate underreporting from overdiagnosis.

Finds 37.2% of the coded long COVID cohort lacked any recorded acute-infection date and that the diagnosis code itself was unavailable for about 2 years, both consistent with undercounting of the true patient population.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers trace the undercounting to a systemic coding or data-infrastructure gap rather than treating it as simply a lack of disease.

evidence.note: Shows only 43.0% of 672 medical records meeting clinical case criteria actually contained the Lyme-specific ICD code, and calls for improved electronic medical/laboratory systems.
Shows no dedicated ICD-10-CM code existed for nearly two years after patients began reporting long COVID symptoms, and that clinicians still struggle to apply the resulting code consistently.

shared_themes.theme: Neither paper provides any dollar cost, income-loss, or caregiving-time figures, so neither can be used alone to size the financial burden on patients.

evidence.note: States explicitly that no direct medical cost, indirect cost, or caregiving burden data are reported anywhere in the document.
States explicitly that no direct medical cost, non-medical cost, indirect cost, or individual-level financial burden data are reported anywhere in the document.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper quantifies a large, specific numeric gap (a 13.62-fold difference) between claims-based diagnosis estimates and official surveillance counts, something the Long COVID paper does not attempt.

evidence.note: Reports a diagnosis-to-surveillance ratio of 13.62 and a raw gap of 441,744.19 patients/year between the claims-based estimate and surveillance-reported cases.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper raises the possibility of overdiagnosis/overtreatment alongside underreporting, a dynamic not discussed in the Long COVID paper.

evidence.note: Notes that 19% of claims-identified diagnoses occurred in low-incidence states (versus a typical surveillance share of about 5%), suggesting possible overdiagnosis contributing to the gap alongside underreporting.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper documents who is demographically left out of the diagnosed/counted population, a dimension the Lyme disease paper does not examine.

evidence.note: Finds the coded cohort was 11.3 percentage points more female and 10.7 percentage points more White than the broader SARS-CoV-2-positive population at the same sites.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper identifies a multi-year classification delay as a distinct, named cause of undercounting.

evidence.note: Reports about 2 years between patients first describing symptoms and the dedicated U09.9 diagnosis code becoming available in October 2021.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither the Lyme disease paper nor the Long COVID paper reports any direct medical cost, out-of-pocket cost, income-loss, or caregiving-time figures, so neither supports a dollar cost-of-illness comparison on its own.

Neither paper provides individual-level subgroup disaggregation of its core burden estimate (the Lyme disease paper reports no breakdown at all; the Long COVID paper reports only area-level, ecological proxies rather than patient-level financial or employment data).
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, so it describes what these two specific papers show rather than general patterns for either condition. Both papers independently conclude that official counting systems undercount the people actually affected, but they measure this through different lenses: the Lyme disease paper quantifies a large national gap between claims-based diagnosis estimates and surveillance case counts, while the Long COVID paper documents a coding classification delay and demographic/socioeconomic skew in who receives a diagnosis code. Neither paper reports any cost, income-loss, or caregiving-burden figures, so this comparison cannot speak to the financial size of either condition's burden. Any agreement between the two papers on the broad idea of undercounting is a pattern found independently in each paper's own analysis, not confirmation or validation of one by the other.
cross_analysis.limitations: This is a small, non-random sample of uploaded documents -exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, with no papers covering both conditions together- and is not a controlled or systematic comparison; findings reflect only what these two specific papers happened to measure and report.

learning_cards.headline: Claims data can reveal diagnoses surveillance never counts.
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper estimates 476744.19 claims-based diagnosed-and-treated patients per year, a gap of 441744.19 patients above the surveillance-reported count, a 13.62-fold difference.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not compare a claims-based diagnosis estimate to a separate surveillance case count for Long COVID.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers build a claims-based diagnosis estimate and compare it to official surveillance counts to see whether a similar fold-gap exists?

learning_cards.headline: Who ends up coded may not match who got infected.
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper found a sex_representation_gap of 11.3 percentage points (women overrepresented) and a race_representation_gap of 10.7 percentage points (White patients overrepresented) among people coded with U09.9 compared with all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not report any demographic representation gap between diagnosed-and-treated patients and the broader exposed or infected population.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease researchers check whether claims-based diagnosed patients differ by sex or race from estimates of everyone likely exposed or infected?

learning_cards.headline: A new diagnosis code can lag years behind reported symptoms.
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper reports a 2-year gap between symptom reports and the dedicated diagnosis code becoming available, and that 37.2% of U09.9 patients have no recorded acute-infection index date.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not measure any lag between symptom onset and diagnosis-code availability, nor does it report a share of patients missing a key exposure or symptom date.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease data systems check how many diagnosed-and-treated patients lack a recorded tick-exposure or symptom-onset date, similar to the missing index-date figure here?

learning_cards.headline: Diagnoses may cluster in places official counts underweight.
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found that the low-incidence-state diagnosis share exceeds the typical surveillance share by 14 percentage points.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report any geographic concentration figure comparing U09.9 diagnosis shares to expected surveillance-based shares by region.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers test whether U09.9 coding is disproportionately concentrated in areas with lighter testing or reporting infrastructure?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper could borrow the Long COVID paper's attention to who gets coded and how long a code takes to catch up with symptoms, while the Long COVID paper could borrow the Lyme disease paper's approach of sizing the gap between claims-based diagnosis estimates and official surveillance counts.
